pages.title: Bilal Ibn Rabah’s Place in Islam
pages.content:
Bilal ibn Rabah was one of the first seven people who openly said they were Muslims in Mecca. After becoming a Muslim, he never left Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) until his death. He was also the first person to give the Adhan, the call to prayer, in the history of Islam.

Bilal was a black slave. He was born in Mecca. His mother was an Ethiopian woman. His father, Rabah, and his mother, Hamama, were also slaves. So Bilal was born into slavery.

Before Islam, he had no hope of becoming free. People in Mecca thought Bilal was just a poor slave. They thought he had no power and would never become someone important. But Islam made him a free and great man. His story teaches us that skin color or being a slave does not make a person less valuable.

His mother was an Ethiopian woman.

pages.title: The Age of Ignorance
pages.content:
The period before Islam was called the Age of Ignorance, or Jahiliyyah. Many people did not believe in the One and Only Allah. They left the true belief and worshipped idols. There was no real peace and justice in society.

There was a big gap between rich and poor people. Rich people had a lot of money and lived in luxury. They used gold plates and silver cups. But many poor people lived in need. Life was very hard for them.

Mecca was a business city. People bought and sold things there. Some rich people lent money to the poor and wanted more money back. This unfair extra money was called riba. Because of this, the rich became richer and the poor became poorer.

exercises.title: Rich and Poor
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 2.
exercises.question: Some rich people lent money to the poor. What did they want back?
options: the same money, with nothing extra
exercises.explanation: The chapter says some rich people “lent money to the poor and wanted more money back.” Because of this, the rich became richer and the poor became poorer.

feedback.incorrect: Look again at the last paragraph of Chapter 2. What did the rich people want back?

languageFocusExercises.title: Two Different Lives
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 2. Then choose the best answer.
languageFocusExercises.question: “They used gold plates and silver cups. But many poor people lived in need.” What does “But” show here?
options: The second sentence is the reason for the first one.
The second sentence shows a very different situation.
The second sentence happened later in time.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “But” joins two different or opposite ideas. Rich people used gold and silver, but poor people did not have enough. The word shows the big gap between the two groups.

feedback.correct: Correct. “But” shows a different, opposite situation.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph again. Compare the life of the rich people with the life of the poor people.

languageFocusExercises.title: Describing the Past
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Complete the lines with the word bank. Two words are extra.
languageFocusExercises.question: What was life like before Islam?
languageFocusExercises.fillBlanksText: The period before Islam [blank] the Age of Ignorance, or Jahiliyyah. … [blank] no real peace and justice in society. … Rich people had [blank] money and lived in luxury.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Was called” gives the name of something. “There was” says that something existed (or did not exist) in the past; “peace and justice” takes “was”. We say “a lot of money”, not “many money” because we cannot count money like this.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the words for a name, a past situation and a quantity.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first two paragraphs of Chapter 2. Check the word after each blank: “money” cannot follow “many”.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the parts in order to make the sentence from Chapter 2.
languageFocusExercises.question: What happened to the rich and the poor?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Because of this” gives the result of something the writer said before (the unfair extra money). “Became + richer/poorer” shows a change over time.

feedback.correct: Correct. The sentence starts with the cause and ends with the result.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the words that link back to the unfair money. Look at the last sentence of Chapter 2.

pages.title: Slaves in Mecca
pages.content:
In this unfair system, the poor were getting poorer and the rich were getting richer. The people with money were the most powerful people in the city.

Slave markets were very common in Arabia. Mecca was a center for buying and selling slaves. Many slaves from different lands, especially from Abyssinia, lived in the homes of Meccan people.

One of those slaves was Bilal ibn Rabah. His master was Umayya ibn Khalaf. Umayya was one of the richest and most powerful leaders in Mecca. He worshipped idols and became a major enemy of Islam. When Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) started teaching Islam, Umayya wanted this message to stop.

exercises.title: Umayya and Islam
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false? Use Chapter 3.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does It Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 3 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the chapter describe Mecca and its people?

matchingPairs.right: they had less and less

matchingPairs.left: Slave markets were very common in Arabia.
matchingPairs.right: You could find them in many places.

correctAnswer.the most powerful people in the city: stronger than all other people in Mecca
He hoped the teaching would end.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Were getting + poorer/richer” shows a change that continued in the past. “The most + adjective” compares one group with all the others. “Wanted + thing + to + verb” shows what someone wished for.

feedback.correct: Correct. You understood the change, the comparison and the wish.

languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word for each sentence from Chapter 3.

When Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) [choice] teaching Islam, …

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “A center for + -ing” says what a place was important for. “From + place” shows where people came from. After “When” in a past story, use the past form: “When … started …”.

pages.title: Bilal’s Hard Life
pages.content:
Umayya never gave up his hatred of Islam and Muslims. Bilal was a slave of Umayya ibn Khalaf. Umayya was always very unkind to Bilal. Every member of the family was rude to him. They did not respect him as a person.

They called Bilal “the son of the black woman” to hurt his feelings. He had a very difficult life at his master’s house. He looked after his master’s camels and worked under the hot sun in the desert of Mecca all day.

In the evening, his job was to bring food and wine to his master. His master was often angry and harsh. No one could say “No” to him or say anything negative. Bilal had to be patient and work hard every day.

exercises.instructions: Match each part with what happened to Bilal in Chapter 4.
exercises.question: What was Bilal’s life like at his master’s house?

matchingPairs.right: He looked after the camels under the hot sun.

They were rude to him and called him names.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4 describes Bilal’s hard work all day, his job in the evening and how the family treated him.

feedback.correct: Well done! You found his work, his evening job and how the family treated him.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the time words in Chapter 4: “all day” and “in the evening”. Then find how the family behaved.

languageFocusExercises.title: How Often, or What Job?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put each part in the right group: How often, or his job.
languageFocusExercises.question: Does it say how often, or what Bilal had to do?

items: Umayya was always very unkind to Bilal.
His master was often angry and harsh.
… worked under the hot sun in the desert of Mecca all day.
He looked after his master’s camels …
… his job was to bring food and wine to his master.
Bilal had to be patient …

How often or how long: Umayya was always very unkind to Bilal.
His master was often angry and harsh.
… worked under the hot sun in the desert of Mecca all day.
Bilal’s job or duty: He looked after his master’s camels …
… his job was to bring food and wine to his master.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Always”, “often” and “all day” tell us how often or how long. “His job was to + verb” and “had to + verb” tell us what Bilal must do. “Had to” shows a past duty: There was no other choice.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated time words from job and duty words.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “always”, “often” and “all day”. Then look for “his job was to” and “had to”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
languageFocusExercises.question: Can you fix the sentences about how people treated Bilal?

errorItems.sentence: They called Bilal “the son of the black woman” for hurt his feelings.
They did not respected him as a person.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Use “to + base verb” to say why someone did something: “to hurt his feelings”. After “did not”, use the base verb: “did not respect”.

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed both sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with Chapter 4: the first paragraph (“did not …”) and the start of the second paragraph (why they called him names).

languageFocusExercises.title: Every Member
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 4. Then choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Every member of the family was rude to him.” What does this mean?
options: Only one person in the family was rude to Bilal.
The family was rude to Bilal only on some days.
All the people in the family were rude to Bilal.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Every + singular noun” means all of them, one by one. The noun is singular (“member”) and the verb is singular (“was”), but the meaning is “all”.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Every member” means all the people in the family.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph again. “Every” does not mean “one” or “sometimes”.

pages.title: A New Message
pages.content:
Umayya liked Bilal because he worked hard and always did what Umayya said. Bilal had to work very hard to please his master and protect himself from his master’s anger.

Bilal thought he would be a slave forever. He did not have any money to pay for his freedom. He also had no power to protect himself from bad behavior.

One day, Bilal heard some people. They were talking about a new Prophet, Muhammad (pbuh). The Prophet (pbuh) was telling everyone to worship only Allah. He taught that people must be fair and equal. He told the people of Mecca to stop worshipping idols. He said, “Worship One Allah. Allah created the world.”

languageFocusExercises.title: Bilal’s Situation

pages.title: Visiting Abu Bakr
pages.content:
Bilal thought about the message of Islam for many days. He walked in the desert all day and thought deeply about the Creator and the creation.

Bilal decided to visit Abu Bakr, the close friend of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh). It was night time and very dark. Bilal felt fear in his heart. He left his room secretly and walked on a hidden path. He did not want anyone to see him.

Bilal knew that Abu Bakr believed in Muhammad’s (pbuh) message. When he arrived at Abu Bakr’s house, he knocked on the door and went inside. He started to ask many questions about the new religion. Abu Bakr was a very kind man, and everybody knew that he was very nice to slaves.

pages.title: Bilal Accepts Islam
pages.content:
Abu Bakr told Bilal about the new religion. Islam says there is no god but Allah. Allah has no partners or equals, not even a rich master or powerful people.

Bilal told Abu Bakr that he wanted to be a Muslim, too. Abu Bakr supported Bilal and was very happy to hear this.

After Bilal met Abu Bakr, he went back home. He could not sleep during the night. He stayed awake and thought about his life. He knew that life would be difficult after becoming a Muslim. But he also knew that the religion of Allah was the truth. Following this religion was the right thing to do. In the end, he accepted Islam. When Umayya learned this, he became very angry.

pages.title: Allah Is One
pages.content:
Umayya asked Bilal angrily, “Is it true? Did you leave our religion and believe in this magic man Muhammad?” Bilal answered with a strong and sure voice: “Yes, Allah helped me to find the right way. Now I believe in the true religion.”

When Umayya heard this, he went mad with anger. He locked Bilal in a house without food or water. He forced him to look at idols and worship them, but Bilal refused.

Umayya told children to tie ropes around Bilal’s neck and pull him through the city of Mecca. He whipped Bilal and put a huge burning rock on his chest in the hot sun. He told him, “If you speak well of our idols, you will be free.” But Bilal only said, “Allah is One, Allah is One.”

languageFocusExercises.title: Forced, but Refused
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence from Chapter 8. Is the statement true or false?
languageFocusExercises.question: “He forced him to look at idols and worship them, but Bilal refused.” This means Bilal did what Umayya wanted.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Forced + person + to + verb” means someone tried to make another person do something with pressure. “Refused” means said no. “But” shows that Bilal did not do what Umayya wanted.

feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph again. What does Bilal do after “but”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Find and Fix the Mistake
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.

errorItems.sentence: Umayya asked Bilal angrily, “Is it true? Did you left our religion and believe in this magic man Muhammad?”

languageFocusExercises.explanation: In a past question, use “Did + person + base verb”: “Did you leave …?” With “If + present”, use “will + verb” for the future result: “If you speak …, you will be free.”

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed the question and the if-sentence.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with Chapter 8: Umayya’s question in the first paragraph and his words in the last paragraph.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Helped + person + to + verb” shows help with an action. “Now + present verb” shows the situation at this moment. “When + past verb” tells us the time of another past action.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right form each time.

pages.title: Abu Bakr Saves Bilal
pages.content:
Umayya wanted Bilal to feel sorry and leave his new religion. But Bilal never said the words that Umayya wanted to hear.

Abu Bakr heard that Umayya was hurting Bilal very badly. He went to see Umayya right away. Bilal was in pain under a heavy rock. Abu Bakr asked Umayya to sell Bilal to him. Umayya did not want to set Bilal free. He was angry and said, “If you want him, you can take him for a high price.”

Abu Bakr asked, “What did he do wrong? Is it a crime to believe in the one true Allah?” But Umayya said, “He is my slave. I can do whatever I want with him.” Again, Abu Bakr asked Umayya to sell Bilal to him.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:mecca-umayya-ibn-khalaf

exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 9.
exercises.question: What did Abu Bakr ask Umayya?
options: “Is it a crime to believe in the one true Allah?”
“Can Bilal work with my camels for one day?”
exercises.explanation: Abu Bakr asked, “What did he do wrong? Is it a crime to believe in the one true Allah?” He showed that Bilal did nothing wrong.

feedback.correct: Yes! Abu Bakr showed that believing in Allah is not a crime.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the last paragraph of Chapter 9. Find Abu Bakr’s question with a question mark.

languageFocusExercises.title: What Does It Mean?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Match each phrase from Chapter 9 with its meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: What do these phrases tell us about Abu Bakr and Umayya?

matchingPairs.left: Abu Bakr heard that Umayya was hurting Bilal
matchingPairs.right: news of the pain reached Abu Bakr
at once, without waiting

matchingPairs.left: Umayya did not want to set Bilal free.
matchingPairs.right: He was not ready to let Bilal go.
for a lot of money

correctAnswer.Abu Bakr heard that Umayya was hurting B: news of the pain reached Abu Bakr
He was not ready to let Bilal go.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Heard that + sentence” reports news someone received. “Right away” shows a very quick action. “Did not want to + verb” shows that someone was not willing to do something.

feedback.correct: Correct. You understood the news, the quick action and Umayya’s answer.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 9 again. Which phrase is about time? Which is about money?

languageFocusExercises.title: Asking for Something
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Put the parts in order to make the sentence from Chapter 9.
languageFocusExercises.question: What did Abu Bakr ask Umayya to do?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Asked + person + to + verb” reports a request. The person who must act (Umayya) comes after “asked”.

feedback.incorrect: Start with the person who asks. Then put the person who must act, then “to + verb”.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Past questions use question word + did + person + base verb: “What did he do …?” After “did”, the verb does not change.

pages.title: A Free Muslim
pages.content:
Finally, Umayya agreed to sell Bilal for five pieces of gold. He laughed at Abu Bakr and said, “Even if you offer me only one piece of gold, I will still sell him to you.” Abu Bakr replied, “Even if you ask me for one hundred pieces of gold, I will still pay that price for him.”

Abu Bakr went to Bilal. Bilal was in great pain. Abu Bakr moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest. Bilal stood up with difficulty. But he went to see Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) first with Abu Bakr.

Abu Bakr told Bilal, “You are a free man now. You are no longer a slave.” Abu Bakr bought Bilal and rescued him from his master’s hands. After that day, Bilal became a free Muslim. He could worship Allah freely. Abu Bakr could keep Bilal as a slave, but he did not. He made him free.

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:mecca-umayya-ibn-khalaf
Said yes.
A valuable yellow metal.
Saved from danger.
Without being forced or stopped.

hotspots.title: Freedom
hotspots.description: Abu Bakr told Bilal that he was now a free man.

hotspots.title: Rescue
hotspots.description: Abu Bakr bought Bilal and rescued him from his master.

exercises.title: The Price
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 10.
exercises.question: In the end, how many pieces of gold did Umayya sell Bilal for?
exercises.explanation: Umayya sold Bilal for five pieces of gold. “One” and “one hundred” are in the chapter too, but they are only what Umayya and Abu Bakr said: “Even if you offer me …” and “Even if you ask me for …”.

feedback.correct: Well done! Five pieces of gold. The other numbers were only words, not the real price.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first sentence of Chapter 10 again: “Umayya agreed to sell Bilal for …”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Real or Imagined?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Real or only words? Put each part in the right group.
languageFocusExercises.question: Did it really happen, or did someone only say it?

items: Umayya agreed … for five pieces of gold.
Abu Bakr moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest.
Bilal stood up with difficulty.
Even if you offer me only one piece of gold, I will still sell him to you.
Even if you ask me for one hundred pieces of gold, I will still pay that price for him.

Really happened: Umayya agreed … for five pieces of gold.
Abu Bakr moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest.
Only words: Even if you offer me only one piece of gold, I will still sell him to you.
Even if you ask me for one hundred pieces of gold, I will still pay that price for him.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Even if you offer …, I will still …” means that the price does not change the answer. These are only words, not real events. The real price was five pieces of gold. Nobody offered one piece or asked for one hundred.

feedback.correct: Correct. You separated real events from words.
feedback.incorrect: Look for “Even if … still …”. These sentences talk about a different price. What was the real price?

languageFocusExercises.title: Agreement and Freedom
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct word or words for each sentence from Chapter 10.
languageFocusExercises.question: How did Bilal become free, and what could he do?

formChoices.sentence: Finally, Umayya agreed [choice] Bilal for five pieces of gold.
Abu Bakr told Bilal, “You are a free man now. You are no [choice] a slave.”
He [choice] worship Allah freely.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: After “agreed”, use “to + verb”. “No longer” shows that an old state has ended: Bilal was not a slave any more. “Could + verb” shows a past ability: now he was able to worship freely.

feedback.correct: Correct. You chose the right form each time.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first and last paragraphs of Chapter 10. The story is in the past, so use the past form of “can”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Could, but Did Not
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentences from Chapter 10. Then choose the best meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Abu Bakr could keep Bilal as a slave, but he did not. He made him free.” What does this tell us?
options: Abu Bakr was not able to keep Bilal.
Abu Bakr wanted to keep Bilal, but Umayya stopped him.
Keeping Bilal was possible, but Abu Bakr chose to free him.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Could + verb, but did not” shows that something was possible, but the person chose not to do it. It shows Abu Bakr’s good choice.

feedback.correct: Correct. It was possible, but Abu Bakr made a better choice.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last three sentences of Chapter 10. “Could” means it was possible. What did Abu Bakr choose?

pages.title: The First Call to Prayer
pages.content:
After Bilal became free, he became one of the Prophet’s most beloved and respected friends. When the Prophet (pbuh) wanted to be alone, he often allowed only Bilal to stay with him.

After many years of hardship in Mecca, the Prophet (pbuh) told the Muslims to move to Medina. After the Hijrah, the Prophet (pbuh) wanted someone to call people to prayer. He chose Bilal.

Bilal was a very brave man. Even when people hurt him, he shouted fearlessly, “There is no god but Allah.” That is why Bilal was the right person to give the first Adhan (call to prayer). So Bilal gave the first Adhan: “Allah is the greatest, Allah is the greatest.”

vocabulary.definition: __historical_entity__:mecca-mecca-7th-century
__historical_entity__:mecca-medina-7th-century
Loved very much.
A difficult time or problem.
The move of the Muslims from Mecca to Medina.
Bravely, not afraid of anyone.

hotspots.title: Hijrah
hotspots.description: The Muslims moved from Mecca to Medina after years of hardship.

hotspots.title: The First Adhan
hotspots.description: The Prophet (pbuh) chose Bilal to call people to prayer.

exercises.title: The First Adhan
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer from Chapter 11.
exercises.question: Why was the first Adhan right for Bilal?
options: He was the oldest Muslim in Medina, and everyone in the city knew him.
He was brave and said “There is no god but Allah” even when people hurt him.
He asked the Prophet (pbuh) for this job many times, and finally he got it.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11 says Bilal was very brave: “Even when people hurt him, he shouted fearlessly, ‘There is no god but Allah.’ That is why Bilal was the right person to give the first Adhan (call to prayer).”

feedback.correct: Right! His brave voice for Allah made him the right person for the first Adhan.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 11 again. Find the words “That is why …”.

pages.title: Prayer Is Better Than Sleep
pages.content:
Bilal used to start the morning call to prayer very early. He added the words “as-salatu khayrun minan-nawm,” which means “Prayer is better than sleep.” The Prophet (pbuh) was pleased with this and told him to repeat it every morning.

Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) taught that all people are equal. No skin color is better than another. Before he died in 632, he gave his last speech. This speech is called the Farewell Sermon.

In this speech, he said it is wrong to dislike or disrespect people because of the color of their skin. He taught that all people come from the same parents, Adam and Eve.

pages.title: Everyone Is Equal
pages.content:
No person is better than another because of skin color. Arabs are not better than non-Arabs, and white people are not better than black people. The only way to be better is to be good and do good actions.

Bilal loved the Prophet (pbuh) very much. When the Prophet (pbuh) died, Bilal was too sad to give the Adhan. He started crying when he said the Prophet’s name. He could not stay in Medina, so he asked Abu Bakr to let him leave. Abu Bakr allowed him to leave the city. He went to Damascus and died there.

Bilal’s story shows that in Islam, everyone is equal. His life teaches us that it is unfair to behave badly to people because of their skin color or nationality. A person’s skin color or past is not important. What matters is the heart and good actions.

places.name: Mecca
places.text: Bilal was born in Mecca. Mecca was a business city. People bought and sold things there.
places.teacherNote: Chapters 1–10 happen in Mecca: Umayya’s house, the desert of Mecca and Abu Bakr’s house. The book does not name these places, so the map shows only the city.
places.question: Why was life hard for Bilal in Mecca?

places.name: Arabia
places.text: Slave markets were very common in Arabia. Mecca was a center for buying and selling slaves.
places.teacherNote: The circle is only approximate. The A2 book does not describe Arabia; it only mentions its slave markets (chapter 3).
places.question: What was very common in Arabia at that time?

places.name: Abyssinia
places.text: Bilal’s mother was an Ethiopian woman. Many slaves in the homes of Meccan people came from Abyssinia. But Bilal was born in Mecca.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 1 says “Ethiopian” and chapter 3 says “Abyssinia”. Bilal himself was born in Mecca, so the map draws no journey for him from here. The circle is approximate.
places.question: Where was Bilal born: in Abyssinia or in Mecca?

places.name: Medina
places.text: After many years of hardship in Mecca, the Muslims moved to Medina. After the Hijrah, Bilal gave the first Adhan. When the Prophet (pbuh) died, Bilal could not stay in Medina.
places.teacherNote: The move to Medina is called the Hijrah (chapter 11). The book gives no year for it. The line from Mecca is only a guide.
places.question: Who gave the first Adhan after the Hijrah?

places.name: Damascus
places.text: The Prophet (pbuh) died in 632. Bilal was very sad. He left Medina and went to Damascus. He died there.
places.teacherNote: Chapter 12 gives the year 632. Chapter 13 gives no year for Bilal’s journey or his death, and no route. The line on the map is only a guide.

exercises.title: What People Thought
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: People in Mecca thought Bilal would never become someone important. What does the story show?
options: He stayed a poor slave all his life.
Islam made him a free and great man.
He became a rich man in Mecca.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1: “They thought he had no power and would never become someone important. But Islam made him a free and great man.”

exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: In Mecca, the rich people also had the most power.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “The people with money were the most powerful people in the city.” Umayya was one of them: He was “one of the richest and most powerful leaders in Mecca.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. In Mecca, money and power went together. That is why life was so hard for the poor.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at the first paragraph of Chapter 3. Who were the most powerful people in the city?

exercises.title: Hard Work
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Why did Bilal work so hard every day?
options: He wanted to save money and buy his freedom.
Umayya promised to make him a free man.
He wanted to please his master and stay safe.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Bilal had to work very hard to please his master and protect himself from his master’s anger.” He could not buy his freedom: “He did not have any money to pay for his freedom.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Bilal worked hard to please Umayya and to be safe from his anger. He had no money and no power.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 5 again. Why did Bilal have to work very hard?

exercises.title: A Long Night
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: After Bilal met Abu Bakr, he could not sleep that night.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “He could not sleep during the night. He stayed awake and thought about his life.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. Bilal could not sleep. He stayed awake and thought about his life and his big decision.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 7 again. What did Bilal do during the night?

exercises.title: Bilal’s Answer
exercises.instructions: Read the question. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Umayya asked Bilal angrily about his new religion. How did Bilal answer?
options: He answered with a strong and sure voice.
He answered with a quiet and afraid voice.
He did not answer and looked away.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 8: “Bilal answered with a strong and sure voice: “Yes, Allah helped me to find the right way. Now I believe in the true religion.””

feedback.correct: Yes. Bilal was not afraid to say the truth, even to his angry master.
feedback.incorrect: Not this one. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 8 again. How did Bilal answer Umayya?

exercises.title: One Hundred Pieces of Gold
exercises.instructions: Read Abu Bakr’s words. Choose the answer.
exercises.question: Abu Bakr said, “Even if you ask me for one hundred pieces of gold, I will still pay that price for him.” What does this show?
options: Abu Bakr had a lot of gold and liked to spend it.
Bilal’s freedom was more important to him than money.
Abu Bakr wanted to pay less than Umayya asked.
exercises.explanation: In Chapter 10, Umayya laughs and says he will still sell Bilal for only one piece of gold. Abu Bakr answers that he will still pay even one hundred. For Abu Bakr, Bilal was worth any price.

feedback.correct: Yes. Umayya thought Bilal was worth very little. Abu Bakr showed that Bilal’s freedom was worth more than any money.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the first paragraph of Chapter 10 again. Compare what Umayya says with what Abu Bakr says.

exercises.title: A Close Friend
exercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: After Bilal became free, the Prophet (pbuh) trusted him and kept him close.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 11: “After Bilal became free, he became one of the Prophet’s most beloved and respected friends. When the Prophet (pbuh) wanted to be alone, he often allowed only Bilal to stay with him.”

feedback.correct: Right, it is true. Bilal was one of the Prophet’s most loved friends. Often, only Bilal could stay with him.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 11 again. Who could stay with the Prophet (pbuh) when he wanted to be alone?

exercises.title: After the Prophet (pbuh)

options: Abu Bakr chose another man to give it in Medina.

pages.title: Language Review
pages.content: Review and use the grammar patterns and language functions from all thirteen chapters.

exercises.title: Look: Again and Again, or One Time?
exercises.instructions: Put each sentence in the right group.
exercises.question: Did it happen again and again, or only one time?

items: Umayya was always very unkind to Bilal.
… the Prophet (pbuh) often allowed only Bilal to stay with him.
Bilal used to start the morning call to prayer very early.
One day, Bilal heard some people …
In the end, Bilal accepted Islam.
Before the Prophet (pbuh) died in 632, he gave his last speech.

Again and again (a habit): Umayya was always very unkind to Bilal.
… the Prophet (pbuh) often allowed only Bilal to stay with him.
Bilal used to start the morning call to prayer very early.
One time (one event): One day, Bilal heard some people …
In the end, Bilal accepted Islam.
Before the Prophet (pbuh) died in 632, he gave his last speech.

exercises.explanation: “Always” and “often” tell us how often. “Used to + verb” tells us about a habit in the past: Bilal started the call to prayer early on many mornings. Time words like “One day”, “In the end” and “Before he died” point to one event at one time.

feedback.correct: Well done. You found the habits and the single events.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the small time words: always, often, used to … or One day, In the end, Before … . Check Chapters 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12.

exercises.title: Look: Had To, Could, Would
exercises.instructions: Match each sentence from the book with its meaning.
exercises.question: What do “had to”, “could” and “would” mean here?

matchingPairs.left: Bilal had to be patient and work hard every day.
matchingPairs.right: There was no other way for him.

matchingPairs.left: He could not sleep during the night.
matchingPairs.right: Sleep was impossible for him.
Now nothing stopped him.

matchingPairs.left: Bilal thought he would be a slave forever.
matchingPairs.right: This was his idea about his future.

correctAnswer.Bilal had to be patient and work hard ev: There was no other way for him.
correctAnswer.Bilal thought he would be a slave foreve: This was his idea about his future.

exercises.explanation: “Had to + verb” shows a past duty: there was no choice. “Could + verb” shows that someone was able to do something; “could not” shows that it was not possible. After “thought” or “knew”, “would + verb” tells us what a person expected for the future.

feedback.correct: Correct. Had to = no choice, could = able, could not = not possible, would = the expected future.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the small verb in each sentence: had to, could, could not, would. Is it about a duty, being able, or the future?

exercises.title: Look: If … and Even If …
exercises.instructions: Read the two sentences. Then choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Chapter 8: “If you speak well of our idols, you will be free.” Chapter 10: “Even if you offer me only one piece of gold, I will still sell him to you.” In which sentence does the answer stay the same, whatever happens?
exercises.explanation: “If …, will …” gives a condition: Bilal will be free only if he speaks well of the idols. “Even if …, will still …” says that the result does not change: Umayya will sell Bilal even for one piece of gold.

feedback.correct: Correct. Even if … still means that the answer does not change.
feedback.incorrect: Look at “even” and “still” in the Chapter 10 sentence. Does the price change Umayya’s answer?

exercises.title: Practise: But, So, Because
exercises.instructions: Complete the lines with the word bank. Two words are extra.
exercises.question: Does each gap need a reason, a result or a different idea?
exercises.fillBlanksText: People in Mecca thought Bilal was just a poor slave. … [blank] Islam made him a free and great man. … Some rich people lent money to the poor and wanted more money back. … [blank], the rich became richer and the poor became poorer. … Umayya liked Bilal [blank] he worked hard and always did what Umayya said. … He could not stay in Medina, [blank] he asked Abu Bakr …
exercises.explanation: “But” gives a different idea: People thought he was just a poor slave, but Islam made him free and great. “Because of this” and “so” give a result. “Because” + a sentence gives the reason. “Because of” needs a noun after it (“because of skin color”), not a sentence.

feedback.correct: Well done. You linked different ideas, reasons and results.
feedback.incorrect: For each gap, ask: Does the next part give a different idea, a reason or a result? Is there a sentence or only a noun after the gap?

exercises.title: Practise: Wanted Him To …, Let Him …
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct form to complete each sentence from the book.
exercises.question: After “forced him”, “wanted Bilal” and “let him”: “to” or no “to”?

formChoices.sentence: He forced him [choice] at idols and worship them …
Umayya wanted Bilal [choice] sorry and leave his new religion.
… he asked Abu Bakr to let him [choice].

exercises.explanation: After “force”, “want”, “ask”, “tell” or “allow” + person, use “to + verb”: “forced him to look”, “wanted Bilal to feel”. After “let” + person, use the base verb without “to”: “let him leave”.

feedback.correct: Correct. Force, want and ask + person + to + verb; let + person + base verb.
feedback.incorrect: Look at the verb before the person: forced, wanted or let? Check Chapters 8, 9 and 13.

exercises.title: Practise: Fix One Mistake
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake. Tap it, then choose the correct words.
exercises.question: Can you fix the verbs in these past sentences?

errorItems.sentence: He leaved his room secretly and walked on a hidden path.
Umayya did not wanted to set Bilal free.
Abu Bakr buyed Bilal and rescued him from his master’s hands.

exercises.explanation: “Leave” and “buy” change in the past: left, bought (not leaved, buyed). Many other verbs just add -ed: walked, rescued. After “did not”, use the base verb: “did not want” (no -ed).

feedback.correct: Well done. You fixed all three sentences.
feedback.incorrect: Compare with the book: Chapter 6 (the hidden path), Chapter 9 (set Bilal free) and Chapter 10 (rescued him).

exercises.title: Practise: One of the Most …
exercises.instructions: Put the parts in order to make the sentence from Chapter 11.
exercises.question: What did Bilal become after he was free?
sentenceChunks: the Prophet’s most beloved and respected
exercises.explanation: “One of the + most … / -est + plural noun” puts one person in a top group: “one of the Prophet’s most beloved and respected friends”. The noun at the end is plural. Chapter 3 uses the same pattern for Umayya: “one of the richest and most powerful leaders in Mecca”.

feedback.correct: Well done. One of + most … + plural noun puts Bilal in a top group.
feedback.incorrect: Start with the time: After Bilal became free. Then say what he became: One of … friends.

exercises.title: Use: A New Student
exercises.instructions: Complete this new text from the word bank. Two words are extra.
exercises.question: Can you use the book’s words in a school story?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Deniz is a new student from another country. On her first day, she could not [blank] the lessons, and she was very quiet. Our teacher asked us [blank] help her. [blank], we sat with her at lunch every day. Now she is one of the happiest [blank] in our class.
exercises.explanation: “Could not” takes the base verb: “could not understand”. “Asked + person + to + verb” reports a request. “Because of this” gives the result. After “one of the happiest”, the noun is plural: “students”. A small kind action can change a new student’s day.

feedback.correct: Well done. You used the book’s language in a new place.
feedback.incorrect: Ask for each gap: Which form comes after could not? after asked us? Is it a result? After one of the …, one or many?

exercises.title: Use: Someone Helped Me
exercises.instructions: Tell a partner. Then write 4–5 sentences about someone who helped.
exercises.question: Who helped you with a problem?
exercises.explanation: Example: “Last year, I was often late for school. I had to take two buses, and I could not wake up early. My brother told me to go to bed at ten, and my mother let me use her alarm clock. Because of this, I am never late now. My mornings are easier than before.”

feedback.correct: Check your sentences: often / used to, had to, could not, told / asked me to …, let me …, because / so / because of this, -er than.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 1 — Give a past habit: “Last year, I was often …” or “I used to …”
discussionPrompts.example: Last year, I was often tired in maths lessons.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 2 — Give the problem: “I had to …, and I could not …”
discussionPrompts.example: I had to do a lot of homework, and I could not understand the lessons.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 3 — Say who helped: “My … told me to … / asked me to … / let me …”
discussionPrompts.example: My sister told me to study with her every evening.

discussionPrompts.question: Sentence 4 — Give the result: “Because of this, … . Now my … is/are …-er than before.”
discussionPrompts.example: Because of this, I understand more now. Now my marks are higher than before.

exercises.title: Born a Slave

options: He came to Mecca from Abyssinia.
He paid for his freedom with gold.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 1 says: “His father, Rabah, and his mother, Hamama, were also slaves. So Bilal was born into slavery.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Bilal did not choose this life. He was a slave from the day he was born.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 1. What does the word “So” tell us?

feedback.correct: True. The rich lived in luxury, but many poor people lived in need.
feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 2. What did rich people use?

exercises.title: Fair and Equal
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: What did the Prophet (pbuh) teach about people?
options: They must be fair and equal.
They must work for rich masters.
They must stay in their own city.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5 says: “The Prophet (pbuh) was telling everyone to worship only Allah. He taught that people must be fair and equal.”

feedback.correct: Yes. This was good news for a slave like Bilal.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last paragraph of Chapter 5. What did the Prophet (pbuh) teach?

exercises.title: No Partners
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 7 with one word: partners, houses or children.
exercises.question: What did Abu Bakr tell Bilal about Allah?
exercises.fillBlanksText: Allah has no [blank] or equals, not even a rich master or powerful people.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7 says: “Islam says there is no god but Allah. Allah has no partners or equals, not even a rich master or powerful people.”

feedback.correct: Yes. No one is equal to Allah, not even a rich master like Umayya.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 7. What does Allah not have?

exercises.title: Who Did It?
exercises.instructions: Match each person with what they did.
exercises.question: Who did these things in the story?

matchingPairs.right: walked on a hidden path at night
locked Bilal in a house without food or water
moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest
chose Bilal to call people to prayer

correctAnswer.Bilal: walked on a hidden path at night
correctAnswer.Umayya: locked Bilal in a house without food or water
correctAnswer.Abu Bakr: moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest
correctAnswer.The Prophet (pbuh): chose Bilal to call people to prayer

exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “He left his room secretly and walked on a hidden path.” Chapter 8: “He locked Bilal in a house without food or water.” Chapter 10: “Abu Bakr moved the heavy rock from Bilal’s chest.” Chapter 11: “the Prophet (pbuh) wanted someone to call people to prayer. He chose Bilal.”

feedback.correct: Yes. You remembered who did each thing in the story.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 6, 8, 10 and 11.

exercises.title: My Slave
exercises.instructions: Choose the best answer.
exercises.question: Umayya said, “He is my slave. I can do whatever I want with him.” What does this show?
options: He wanted to sell Bilal for one piece of gold.
He was afraid of Abu Bakr.
He did not see Bilal as a person with rights.
exercises.explanation: In Chapter 9 Abu Bakr asks: “Is it a crime to believe in the one true Allah?” Umayya answers: “He is my slave. I can do whatever I want with him.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Umayya thought a master could do anything to a slave.
feedback.incorrect: Read Umayya’s answer at the end of Chapter 9. How did he see Bilal?

exercises.title: After the Sale
exercises.instructions: Is the sentence true or false?
exercises.question: Abu Bakr bought Bilal and kept him as his own slave.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 10 says: “Abu Bakr could keep Bilal as a slave, but he did not. He made him free.”

feedback.correct: Right. Abu Bakr did not buy Bilal to own him. He bought him to free him.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last two sentences of Chapter 10. What did Abu Bakr do?

exercises.title: Places in the Story
exercises.instructions: Match each place with what the story says about it.
exercises.question: What happened in each place?

matchingPairs.right: a center for buying and selling slaves
a land many slaves came from
the city where Bilal gave the first Adhan
the city where Bilal died

correctAnswer.Mecca: a center for buying and selling slaves
correctAnswer.Abyssinia: a land many slaves came from
correctAnswer.Medina: the city where Bilal gave the first Adhan

exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “Mecca was a center for buying and selling slaves. Many slaves from different lands, especially from Abyssinia, lived in the homes of Meccan people.” Chapter 11: after the Hijrah to Medina, “So Bilal gave the first Adhan”. Chapter 13: “He went to Damascus and died there.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Bilal’s life moved from Mecca to Medina, and it ended in Damascus.
feedback.incorrect: Look again at Chapters 3, 11 and 13.

exercises.title: The Way to Be Better
exercises.instructions: Complete the sentence from Chapter 13 with one word: actions, clothes or money.
exercises.question: What is the only way to be better?
exercises.fillBlanksText: The only way to be better is to be good and do good [blank].
exercises.explanation: Chapter 13 says: “No person is better than another because of skin color. … The only way to be better is to be good and do good actions.”

feedback.correct: Yes. Skin color does not make a person better. Good actions do.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 13. What makes a person better?

exercises.title: Bilal’s Journey
exercises.instructions: Put these events in the order of the story.
exercises.question: What happened first, next and last?

sequencingItems.text: Umayya locks Bilal in a house.
Bilal learns about a new Prophet.
Bilal visits Abu Bakr at night.
Abu Bakr buys Bilal for five pieces of gold.

exercises.explanation: The new Prophet (Chapter 5), the night visit (Chapter 6), Umayya’s anger (Chapter 8), the sale (Chapter 10) and the first Adhan (Chapter 11).

feedback.correct: Yes. Bilal heard the message, suffered for it, became free and then called people to prayer.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that Bilal became free before the Muslims moved to Medina.
